definition: The property that a program only accesses memory inside the bounds and lifetime of the objects it is allowed to use. C and C++ do not enforce it, so bugs such as buffer overflows and use-after-free can corrupt or disclose memory.
example: Chromium reported that around 70% of a sample of 912 high or critical security bugs since 2015 were memory-safety bugs.

definition: Behaviour for which the C or C++ standard imposes no requirements, such as writing past an array or using freed memory. The program might crash, appear to work, or do something an attacker can steer; compilers may also optimise on the assumption it never happens.
example: strcpy into an 8-byte buffer from an 11-byte source has undefined behaviour: no particular crash or overwrite is promised.

definition: The international standard that defines the C programming language. C99, C11 and C17 are editions from 1999, 2011 and 2018 (C17 mostly fixes C11); they say which operations are valid and which have undefined behaviour.
example: The function gets was removed from the library in C11 because it cannot be used safely.

definition: A programming language that extends C with classes, templates and a large standard library. Like C it gives direct access to memory without universal bounds or lifetime checks, so it shares C's memory-safety bugs.

A value holding the memory address of something else, such as a buffer or a function. In C, code can do arithmetic on pointers and follow them without the language checking that the target is still valid.
example: If p points to the start of char buf[16], then p + 15 points at its last byte and p + 16 is one past the end.

definition: A test that an index or length lies inside the object being accessed before the access happens. C does not perform them automatically; the programmer must write them.
example: Before copying len bytes into a 16-byte buffer, check that len ≤ 16.

definition: The period during which an object's storage is validly reserved for it, for example from malloc until free. Using the object outside its lifetime is a temporal memory-safety bug.
example: After free(s), the lifetime of *s has ended even though the pointer s still holds the old address.

definition: A memory-safety bug where an access falls outside the object's bounds, such as a buffer overflow or an out-of-bounds read. The question it breaks is 'is this address inside the object?'.
example: Writing arr[10] in a 10-element array is a spatial error: valid indices are 0 to 9.

definition: A memory-safety bug where an access happens outside the object's lifetime, such as use-after-free or double free. The address may once have been valid, but the object is no longer alive.
example: Reading s->name after free(s) is a temporal error.

definition: An unintended change to memory caused by a bug, such as an overflow writing over neighbouring data. Attackers use it to alter decisions or redirect execution.

How a running program's memory is arranged: code, global data, the heap and the stack placed in separate regions of its address space. Exact placement depends on the operating system, architecture and ASLR.
The region of memory that holds each active function call's local variables, saved registers and return address. On common architectures it grows downwards, towards lower addresses, as calls nest.
example: Calling greet() pushes a new stack frame holding buf[16]; returning pops it.

definition: The block of call-stack memory belonging to one function call: its locals, saved registers and the return address. Overflowing a buffer in a frame can overwrite the other items in it.

The region where a program allocates memory at run time with malloc (or new in C++) and later frees it. Objects there live until explicitly freed, which is where use-after-free and double free bugs arise.
example: malloc(64) returns a pointer to 64 bytes of heap memory.

definition: Regions of a program image holding global and static variables: .data stores those with initial values, .bss those that start as zero. They are writable but, with NX, not executable.
The region of a program image that holds its machine code. It is normally mapped readable and executable but not writable.
CPU register values that a function stores on the stack on entry so it can restore them before returning to its caller.

The address of the instruction a function should continue at after it returns, typically saved on the stack by the call instruction. Overwriting it lets an attacker choose where execution goes when the function returns.
example: On x86-64, call pushes the 8-byte return address and ret pops it into the instruction pointer.

definition: A register value marking the base of a stack frame. A function saves its caller's frame pointer on the stack so the chain of frames can be followed and restored; debuggers can use it to walk the stack.
A variable declared inside a function, which C calls an automatic variable. It normally lives in that call's stack frame (or a register) and disappears when the function returns.
The library code behind malloc and free that hands out heap memory and recycles freed blocks. Its choices about when to reuse memory decide how a use-after-free plays out.
example: glibc's malloc keeps freed chunks on free lists and can hand the same address to the next malloc of a similar size.

definition: Bookkeeping the memory allocator keeps next to or inside heap blocks, such as chunk sizes and free-list pointers. Corrupting it can make later malloc or free calls write attacker-chosen values.

Values that decide where execution goes next, such as return addresses and function pointers. Corrupting them turns a memory bug into control of the program, which is why many mitigations protect them.
The order in which a program's instructions execute, including calls, returns, jumps and branches.
An attack that corrupts control data, such as a return address or function pointer, so the program jumps to a location of the attacker's choosing.
An attack that changes ordinary data, such as an authorisation flag, rather than redirecting execution. Control-flow defences such as canaries, CFI and shadow stacks do not stop it.
example: Overflowing name[16] into the neighbouring is_admin field grants access without touching any return address.

definition: A bug where a program writes past the end (or before the start) of a buffer, overwriting neighbouring memory. Depending on what lies next to the buffer, it can change data, crash the program or redirect execution.
example: Copying a 40-byte name into char buf[16] with strcpy writes 25 bytes past the end.

definition: A buffer overflow in a buffer that lives on the call stack. Because the return address sits in the same stack frame, it is the classic route to hijacking a function's return.

An overflow that writes consecutive bytes onwards from the buffer, so it must pass through everything between the buffer and its target. A stack canary relies on this: the overflow has to cross the canary to reach the return address.

A memory write that lands at a chosen location without touching the bytes in between, for example arr[i] = x with an attacker-controlled index i. It can change a return address while leaving the stack canary intact.
Reading memory outside the object being accessed. If the bytes reach the attacker, it discloses memory, possibly secrets or addresses that weaken ASLR; Heartbleed is the famous case.
example: Heartbleed copied up to 65,535 bytes from a payload that might only be a few bytes long.

definition: A bug where a loop or bound is wrong by exactly one, for example using <= instead of <. With arrays it typically reads or writes one element past the end.
example: for (i = 0; i <= 8; i++) on char id[8] writes id[8], one past the last valid index 7.

definition: An information leak that reveals a memory address, for example through an out-of-bounds read. One leaked pointer into a library reveals where that whole library is loaded, undoing ASLR for it.
A byte whose value is 0. As a character it is called NUL, written '\0' in C; C strings end at the first NUL, so string functions copy or read until they meet one.
example: "abc" occupies 4 bytes: 'a', 'b', 'c' and a NUL.

definition: A sequence of bytes ending in a NUL byte, which is how C represents text. Functions that work on C strings have no separate length and rely on that terminator, so a missing NUL makes them read past the end.
The C library function strcpy(dst, src) that copies a NUL-terminated string, including its NUL, into dst. It is never told dst's size, so too long a source overflows the destination.
example: strcpy into char buf[8] from "ABCDEFGHIJ" needs 11 bytes and overflows by 3.

definition: The C library function strncpy(dst, src, n) that copies at most n bytes. If the source is n bytes or longer it does not add a terminating NUL, and if shorter it pads the rest with NULs, so it is not a safe strcpy.
example: strncpy(dst, "abcdef", 4) leaves dst holding abcd with no NUL.

definition: A bounded string copy, from BSD and now in some other C libraries, that always NUL-terminates when the size is non-zero and returns the source's length so truncation can be detected. It is not part of ISO C, so it is not available everywhere.

The C library function that formats text into a buffer of a given size, never writing more than that size and adding a NUL when the size is non-zero. It returns the length the full output would have needed, so a return equal to or above the size signals truncation.
example: snprintf(d, 8, "%s", "hello world") stores hello w and returns 11.

definition: The C library function that prints text according to a format string, replacing directives such as %s and %d with its further arguments. Passing untrusted text as the format string is the format-string bug.
A C library function that formats text into a buffer like printf but with no size limit, so long output overflows the buffer. snprintf is the bounded replacement.
The C library function that writes a string to a stream exactly as it is, without interpreting % directives. That makes it safe for printing untrusted text.
The C library function memcpy(dst, src, n) that copies exactly n bytes, whatever they contain. It checks nothing, so n must fit both the source and the destination.
example: Heartbleed's bug was a memcpy whose n came from the attacker.

definition: A C library function like memcpy that copies n bytes but also works correctly when the source and destination overlap.
An old C library function that read a line of input into a buffer with no way to give the buffer's size, so any long line overflowed it. It was removed from the language in C11.

Cutting data off at a size limit, keeping only the first part, such as a string shortened to fit a buffer. In C, bounded functions such as snprintf truncate output that does not fit, and code must check for it because silently shortened data can itself cause bugs.
example: Formatting "hello world" into 8 bytes truncates it to hello w.

definition: The unsigned integer type C uses for object sizes and byte counts, returned by sizeof and taken by malloc. It is typically 32 bits on 32-bit platforms and 64 bits on 64-bit ones.
example: With a 32-bit size_t the largest value is 4,294,967,295.

definition: A C constant equal to the largest value size_t can hold: 2^32 − 1 (4,294,967,295) for a 32-bit size_t. Checking count > SIZE_MAX / size before multiplying detects size overflow.
A C operator that gives the size in bytes of a type or object, worked out by the compiler. For an array such as char buf[16], sizeof buf is 16.
C types from <stdint.h> with an exact size: uint8_t is an unsigned 8-bit integer (1 byte), uint32_t 32 bits (4 bytes) and uint64_t 64 bits (8 bytes).
An integer type that holds only zero and positive values. An n-bit unsigned type holds 0 to 2^n − 1, and in C its arithmetic wraps around instead of failing when a result is too big or below zero.
example: A 32-bit unsigned value holds 0 to 4,294,967,295.

definition: When an arithmetic result is too large for its integer type. For unsigned types in C the result silently wraps around; when it feeds a size calculation, a huge request can become a tiny allocation.
example: With a 32-bit size_t, 268,435,457 × 16 wraps to 16.

definition: What an unsigned integer does when a result leaves its range: it keeps only the lowest bits, so counting continues from 0 after the maximum (and from the maximum below 0). For a 32-bit type this is arithmetic modulo 2^32.
example: In 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, 4,294,967,295 + 1 gives 0 and 0 − 1 gives 4,294,967,295.

definition: Subtracting more than an unsigned value holds, so the result wraps around to a huge number instead of going negative. A length check written as len > total − 19 is fooled when total is below 19.
example: With a 32-bit size_t, 10 − 19 gives 4,294,967,287.

definition: The prefix C and most programming tools put before a hexadecimal number, so 0x10 means sixteen rather than ten.
The natural integer and pointer size of a processor: 8 bytes (64 bits) on x86-64 and AArch64. The glibc stack canary is one machine word.
A byte order in which the least significant byte of a multi-byte value is stored at the lowest address. x86-64 and most Arm systems are little-endian.
example: The 4-byte value 0x11223344 is stored as 44 33 22 11.

definition: A temporal memory-safety bug in which a program keeps using a pointer after the memory it points to has been freed. If the allocator has reused that memory for attacker-controlled data, the stale access can read or act on it.
example: A freed session object's memory is reused for request bytes, and a stale check of s->is_admin reads the attacker's byte.

definition: Freeing the same allocation twice, which is undefined behaviour in C. It can corrupt the allocator's bookkeeping or make two later allocations share memory; some allocators detect it and abort.
A pointer that still holds the address of an object whose lifetime has ended, for example after free. Using it is a use-after-free.
A second pointer to the same object. Freeing through one pointer, or setting it to NULL, does nothing to the others, which then dangle.

A rule about which part of a program is responsible for freeing an allocation. Code that only borrows a pointer must not free it or keep it after the owner frees it; clear ownership prevents use-after-free and double free.
A C++ smart pointer that is the single owner of an object and frees it automatically when it goes out of scope. It cannot be copied, only moved, so ownership stays clear.
A C++ smart pointer that shares ownership through a reference count and frees the object when the last shared_ptr to it is destroyed.
A pointer value that points to no object. free(NULL) does nothing, but dereferencing NULL is undefined behaviour, not a guaranteed clean crash.
To follow a pointer and access the object at its address, such as reading s->is_admin through the pointer s.
The C library function that allocates a block of heap memory of a given number of bytes and returns a pointer to it, or NULL on failure. The block must later be released with free.
example: malloc(count * 16) requests 16 bytes per item, unless the multiplication wraps.

definition: A C library function that allocates memory for count items of a given size and zeroes it. glibc's calloc returns NULL instead of wrapping when count × size overflows.
A function, standardised in POSIX but not ISO C, that resizes an array allocation for count items of a given size and fails instead of wrapping when count × size overflows.
Two threads using the same memory at the same time without a lock or other coordination, with at least one writing. In C and C++ it is a data race and undefined behaviour.
A bug where untrusted text is passed as the format argument of printf or a similar function, so % directives in it are interpreted. It can disclose memory or, with %n, attempt a write.
example: printf(user_input) with input %x %x %x may print stack values.

definition: A %-sequence in a printf format string that tells printf to consume an argument, such as %s (a string), %d (an integer), %x (hexadecimal) or %n (store the number of characters printed so far through a pointer).

The rules for how a function receives arguments (which registers or stack slots), returns results and preserves registers on a given architecture. A format-string bug reads whatever happens to be where the missing arguments would be.
A variable read before anything has been stored in it. In C an uninitialised local has an indeterminate value, and many uses of it are undefined behaviour rather than a reliable read of old bytes.
Unused bytes the compiler inserts between or after a struct's fields so each field is aligned. Their contents are not set by assigning the fields, so copying the raw struct out can leak old memory.
example: In struct { uint8_t flag; uint64_t value; }, bytes 1–7 are typically padding, making the struct 16 bytes.

definition: The requirement that a value of a given type starts at an address that is a multiple of some number, often its own size. A uint64_t is typically 8-byte aligned, which is why padding appears before it.
An explicitly defined layout of bytes for sending data between programs, with set field sizes, order and endianness, independent of how a compiler lays out a struct in memory.

A Linux kernel function that copies bytes from kernel memory into a user-space buffer, checking that the destination is a valid user address. Whatever bytes it is given, including struct padding, reach the user program.
Code that runs inside the operating-system kernel to control hardware or provide a service. Bugs in it run with the kernel's full privileges.
The memory and privilege level where ordinary programs run, separated from the kernel. Data passes between them only through controlled interfaces such as system calls.
The core software, such as Linux or Windows, that manages memory, processes and hardware for programs. It sets page permissions and implements ASLR.
A widely used open-source operating-system kernel; GNU/Linux refers to it together with the GNU tools and C library (glibc).

A 2014 OpenSSL vulnerability (CVE-2014-0160): the TLS heartbeat code trusted the length an attacker claimed and copied that many bytes back, leaking up to about 64 KB of server memory per request, including possible private keys and cookies.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a public catalogue that gives each known security vulnerability a unique identifier such as CVE-2014-0160 (Heartbleed).

A TLS extension (RFC 6520) for checking a connection is alive: one side sends a payload and the other echoes it back. A message holds a 1-byte type, a 2-byte payload length, the payload and at least 16 bytes of padding.

The part of a message header that says how long the message's payload (or the whole message) is. In a TLS heartbeat it is 2 bytes counting only the payload, so it can claim up to 65,535 bytes; it must be checked against what actually arrived.

Code that reads structured input, such as a file format or network message, and turns it into data the program uses. Parsers of untrusted input are a prime source of memory-safety bugs and a prime fuzzing target.

A compiler-inserted memory-error detector in Clang and GCC, enabled with -fsanitize=address. It marks memory around and after objects as poisoned in shadow memory and reports accesses to it, catching many overflows and use-after-free bugs on the paths a test runs.
example: ASan reports heap-use-after-free when code reads an object that is still in its freed quarantine.

definition: A Clang and GCC run-time checker that reports certain kinds of undefined behaviour when they happen, such as signed integer overflow or misaligned pointers.
A compiler feature that adds run-time checks to a program to detect a class of bugs while it runs, such as AddressSanitizer for memory errors. It finds bugs only on the paths actually executed.
A separate region of memory that records metadata about the program's own memory. AddressSanitizer uses one shadow byte per 8 application bytes to record which bytes are safe to access.
Marking memory as off-limits, for example the gaps around objects and recently freed blocks, so a checker such as ASan reports any access to it.
A checker or allocator holding freed memory back for a while before handing it out again, so a use-after-free hits poisoned memory and is detected instead of reaching a new object.
Extra checking code inserted into a program, by the compiler or at run time, to observe or verify what it does. Only instrumented code is checked, so uninstrumented libraries can hide bugs.

A tool that runs an unmodified program on a simulated CPU, checking each memory access for errors such as use of freed or uninitialised memory. It needs no recompilation but makes the program much slower.
Adding checks to a compiled program's machine code while it runs, without its source code, as Valgrind does.
Automatically running a program on large numbers of generated or mutated inputs, often malformed, to find crashes and bugs. Combined with sanitizers it exposes memory errors on the paths it reaches.
Fuzzing that measures which code each input exercises and keeps mutating the inputs that reach new code, so it explores a program far more deeply than random inputs.
An in-process, coverage-guided fuzzing engine that is part of LLVM. You write a small function that passes each generated input to the code under test.
A widely used coverage-guided fuzzer, the community successor to American Fuzzy Lop (AFL).
A free Google service that continuously fuzzes eligible open-source projects with sanitizers and reports the bugs it finds to their maintainers.
A collection of sample inputs, such as valid image files, used as tests or as the starting point that a fuzzer mutates.
A test kept to check that behaviour which used to work, or a bug that was fixed, does not break again.
Examining source code for bugs without running it. It can reason about all paths but often reports false positives and misses bugs that depend on run-time values.

GCC and Clang options: -Wall turns on a broad set of common warnings (including -Wformat); -Wformat checks printf-style calls against their format strings; -Wformat-security warns when a non-literal format string has no arguments; and -Werror (or -Werror=format-security) turns warnings into build errors.
An option passed to the compiler or linker on its command line, such as -O2 or -fstack-protector-strong, that changes how a program is built.

How hard the compiler works to make code faster or smaller: -O0 means no optimisation, while -O1 to -O3 enable increasingly aggressive optimisation. Some checks, such as FORTIFY_SOURCE, need optimisation to work.
The GNU Compiler Collection, a widely used open-source compiler for C, C++ and other languages; the default compiler on most Linux distributions.
The C, C++ and Objective-C compiler of the LLVM project. It provides sanitizers and control-flow integrity schemes.
The GNU C Library, the standard C library on most Linux systems. It provides malloc, strcpy, printf and also stack-canary set-up and source fortification.

The C standard library a program links against, providing functions such as malloc, printf and memcpy; on most Linux systems it is glibc. It is mapped into almost every process, which makes it a favourite target for code reuse.
Portable Operating System Interface: an IEEE standard for Unix-like system interfaces, adding functions such as reallocarray that ISO C does not define.
The signal a Unix-like operating system sends a process that touches memory it may not access, which normally terminates it. A crash, not a guaranteed result of a memory bug.
A protection in the compiler, operating system or CPU that makes particular ways of exploiting a bug harder, such as stack canaries or ASLR. It does not fix the bug itself.
Configuring software, its build or a system so that bugs are harder to exploit, for example by enabling stack protection, RELRO and fortification.
The set of programs that turn source code into a running program: compiler, assembler, linker and C library.

A secret random value the compiler places between a function's local buffers and its saved return address, checked before the function returns. A linear overflow that reaches the return address must overwrite it first, so the program aborts instead of returning.
example: With glibc on x86-64 the canary is 8 bytes with its lowest byte set to zero, leaving 56 random bits.

definition: The function that stack-protector code calls when a canary check fails. In glibc it reports stack smashing and aborts the process.

GCC and Clang options that add stack canaries. -fstack-protector protects only functions that call alloca or have stack buffers of at least 8 bytes (GCC's default threshold); -fstack-protector-strong also protects functions with any local array or that take the address of a local variable.
The instructions at the end of a function that restore saved registers and return to the caller. With stack protection, the canary check runs here, just before ret.

A 2014 attack technique (Bittau et al., 'Hacking Blind') against servers that restart crashed workers with the same memory layout. It reads the canary and return addresses a byte at a time from crash or no-crash responses, then builds return-oriented programming chains.
The Unix system call that creates a child process as a copy of the calling process, with the same memory contents and layout, so the child shares the parent's canary and ASLR bases.

A protection that marks memory pages as non-executable, so the CPU refuses to run instructions from data areas such as the stack and heap. NX is the hardware page bit; DEP is Microsoft's name for the feature.
example: Injected machine code on a non-executable stack page faults when the CPU tries to fetch it.

definition: A policy that no page may be both writable and executable at the same time, so code can never be modified where it runs. It is stronger than NX alone, which only prevents executing non-executable pages.
The fixed-size block, typically 4 KiB on x86-64 Linux, in which the operating system maps memory and sets read, write and execute permissions.
The read, write and execute rights set for each memory page. The CPU checks them on every access and faults on a violation.
The CPU reading the next machine instruction from memory before executing it. NX makes this fail on pages not marked executable.
Instructions encoded as bytes the CPU executes directly.
Placing the attacker's own machine code in memory, for example in a buffer, and redirecting execution to it. NX blocks it on non-executable pages.
An attack that redirects execution through instructions already in the program and its libraries instead of injecting new code. Because that code is legitimately executable, NX does not stop it.
A code-reuse attack that places a chain of addresses on the stack, each pointing to a short existing instruction sequence ending in ret, so each return runs the next piece of the attacker's program.
A short instruction sequence already in executable memory that ends in a return instruction. Chained together, gadgets let an attacker perform arbitrary operations without injecting code.
example: A gadget such as pop rdi; ret lets the attacker load a chosen value into a register.

definition: The machine instruction that returns from a function by taking the return address from the stack and jumping to it.

A just-in-time compiler: it turns code into machine code while the program runs, as JavaScript engines do. It therefore needs memory that becomes executable at run time, which must be protected carefully.
A second, writable mapping of memory that is also mapped executable elsewhere. An attacker who can write through it can change code that will run, undermining W^X.

An operating-system protection that loads the stack, heap, libraries and (for PIE programs) the main program at random addresses, so an attacker cannot predict where useful code or data is. A pointer leak can undo it for one mapping.
example: With 28 random bits a library can start at any of 268,435,456 positions.

definition: The range of memory addresses a process can use, each mapped by the operating system to physical memory or nothing. Each process has its own.
A region of a process's address space backed by something, such as a library file or anonymous memory, with its own permissions. ASLR randomises where each mapping starts, its base.
The address where a mapping, such as a shared library, starts in memory. Everything inside sits at a fixed offset from it, so knowing the base locates everything.
The distance in bytes from the start of something, such as a struct or a library, to an item inside it. Library offsets are fixed for a given build, so base + offset gives an item's address.
A Linux setting (sysctl) that chooses how many random bits ASLR uses for the base of mmap-allocated regions, within limits the architecture and kernel build allow.
A Linux interface for reading and changing kernel settings at run time, such as vm.mmap_rnd_bits.
Kernel address space layout randomisation: loading the operating-system kernel itself at a random address at boot. A leaked kernel pointer can reveal the base.
Chosen so that every possible value has the same probability. Independent means each choice is unaffected by the others; together these are the assumptions behind simple 2^b guessing estimates.
The long-run average of a random quantity, such as the number of guesses an attack needs, over many repetitions.
example: Guessing one of 256 fixed candidates in order takes 128.5 attempts on average.

definition: The probability distribution of how many independent tries it takes to get the first success when each try succeeds with probability p. Its mean is 1/p.
example: With a 1-in-256 chance per try, the mean is 256 tries.

definition: Executable and Linkable Format: the file format for programs and shared libraries on Linux and most other Unix-like systems.

A program compiled so its code works at any load address, letting ASLR place the main executable randomly as well as its libraries. A non-PIE executable's main code sits at a fixed address. -fPIE and -pie are the GCC compile and link flags.

Relocation Read-Only: a linker and loader feature that makes an ELF program's relocation data read-only once it has been filled in at start-up. Full RELRO also binds functions eagerly so the GOT can be protected too.
Patching addresses in a program or library when it is loaded, because the final location of code and data, especially with ASLR, is only known then.

A table in an ELF program holding the addresses of external functions and variables, filled in by the dynamic loader. Overwriting an entry redirects every call through it, which full RELRO prevents by making it read-only.
Resolving an external function's address only on its first call, which needs the GOT entry to stay writable while the program runs.

aliases: resolved when the object is loaded
definition: Resolving all of a program's required function addresses when it is loaded instead of on first call, requested with the linker flag -z now. It lets the GOT be made read-only before main runs.
A compiler option that passes -z relro and -z now to the linker (-Wl, means 'pass to the linker'), enabling full RELRO.
Conventional build variables (for example in Makefiles) holding the options passed to the C compiler (CFLAGS) and the linker (LDFLAGS).
The part of the system (ld.so on Linux) that maps a program and its shared libraries into memory at start-up, applies relocations and resolves function addresses.
A function that loads a shared library into a running process on request, after start-up. The new library has its own relocations.
A system call that changes the permissions (read, write, execute) of pages in a process's memory; the loader uses it to make the RELRO region read-only.

A glibc and compiler feature that replaces calls such as memcpy and strcpy with checked versions when the destination's size can be worked out, aborting on overflow. Level 3 also uses sizes known only at run time. It works only in optimised builds.
example: memcpy(dst, src, n) becomes __memcpy_chk(dst, src, n, dst_size), which aborts if n > dst_size.

definition: Compiler built-ins that report how many bytes remain in the object a pointer points to, if the compiler can tell. _FORTIFY_SOURCE uses __builtin_object_size, and at level 3 __builtin_dynamic_object_size, which also handles run-time sizes.
The checked version of memcpy that fortified code calls: it takes the destination's size as an extra argument and aborts if the copy would exceed it.
Application binary interface: the low-level rules a platform's compiled code follows, such as type sizes, struct layout and alignment, calling convention and stack-frame layout.
The 64-bit version of Intel and AMD's x86 processor architecture, used in most PCs and servers. It is little-endian.

A family of protections that check indirect calls, jumps or returns go only to targets the program could legitimately reach, defeating many code-reuse attacks. Schemes differ in which transfers they check and how precisely.
In control-flow integrity, a transfer to a new location chosen at run time: an indirect call or jump. Forward-edge protections include Clang CFI, Microsoft CFG, Intel IBT and Arm BTI.
In control-flow integrity, a return from a function back to its caller. Shadow stacks and pointer authentication protect backward edges.

A call or jump whose destination is read from a register or memory at run time, such as calling through a function pointer, rather than fixed in the instruction. Corrupting that value redirects execution.
A pointer holding the address of a function, used to call it indirectly. Overwriting one makes the next indirect call go wherever the attacker chose.
A C++ method call dispatched at run time through a table of function pointers (the vtable), so it is an indirect call that CFI can protect.

Clang's control-flow integrity schemes, enabled with -fsanitize=cfi. They check that indirect and virtual calls reach a function of the expected type, and need link-time optimisation and suitable visibility settings.
Optimising a whole program at link time, when the compiler can see all its pieces together. Clang CFI needs it to know every valid call target.
Control-flow integrity that allows an indirect call only to functions whose type matches the call site. An attacker can still pick an unintended function of the same type.
A Windows forward-edge protection: the compiler inserts a check before indirect calls that the target is a valid function start, recorded in a bitmap. It is coarser than a type-based check.
A table with one bit per item recording yes or no. Microsoft CFG, for example, uses one to record which addresses are valid indirect-call targets.
Indirect Branch Tracking, part of Intel CET: when enabled, an indirect call or jump must land on an ENDBR64 (or ENDBR32) instruction, otherwise the CPU faults.
Branch Target Identification, an Armv8.5-A feature: on protected pages, indirect branches must land on a BTI landing-pad instruction, otherwise the CPU faults.
The x86 instruction that marks a valid target for indirect branches under Intel IBT. On processors without IBT it does nothing.
A special instruction that marks a place an indirect branch is allowed to arrive, such as ENDBR64 or BTI. Any marked place is accepted, so it is coarser than checking the intended function.

Control-flow Enforcement Technology: Intel processor features providing a hardware shadow stack (for returns) and Indirect Branch Tracking (for indirect calls and jumps); recent AMD processors also implement the shadow stack. Software, kernel and CPU must all support and enable it.
A GCC and Clang option that builds code for Intel CET, adding ENDBR64 landing pads and marking the binary as shadow-stack compatible. Enforcement still depends on the CPU, kernel and runtime.

A second, protected stack that holds only copies of return addresses. On each return the CPU (or code) checks the normal return address against the copy and faults if they differ, stopping return-address overwrites such as ROP.

An Armv8.3-A feature that stores a short keyed cryptographic code in a pointer's unused upper bits and checks it before the pointer is used. A pointer changed by an attacker fails the check. It authenticates pointers but does not encrypt them.

An Armv8.5-A feature that gives every 16-byte granule of memory a 4-bit allocation tag and every pointer a 4-bit tag in its top byte; a checked access faults when they differ. It catches many overflows and use-after-free bugs, probabilistically.
example: With 16 possible tags, a stale pointer matches a randomly retagged granule 1 time in 16.

definition: In MTE, a 4-bit value attached both to a granule of memory (the allocation tag) and to the pointers used to reach it (the pointer tag). Freed memory is retagged, so stale pointers usually carry the wrong tag.
In MTE, the 16-byte block of memory that shares one allocation tag. An overflow that stays inside one granule is not detected.
Ways MTE reports tag mismatches: synchronous mode faults on the exact bad access; asynchronous mode records the fault and reports it later, which is cheaper but lets execution continue for a while.
Changes to a memory allocator that make heap bugs harder to exploit, such as protecting free-list pointers or delaying reuse of freed memory.
A glibc malloc hardening (since glibc 2.32) that scrambles singly linked free-list pointers with bits of their own address, so an overwrite without a heap address leak produces an unusable pointer.
An allocator's list of freed blocks waiting to be reused, linked by pointers stored inside the freed blocks themselves, which makes those pointers a target for heap corruption.

Chrome's MiraclePtr implementation: pointers declared as raw_ptr<T> keep a reference count, and memory freed while such references remain is quarantined and poisoned instead of reused, blunting use-after-free.

Memory whose pages are marked so the CPU may run instructions from it, normally only a program's and its libraries' code. NX keeps data such as the stack and heap out of it, but code-reuse attacks run code that is already executable.

An allocator handing memory that was freed to a later allocation. If a stale pointer still refers to it, that pointer now reaches the new object, often filled with attacker-chosen data, which is what makes use-after-free exploitable.

The compiler stage that produces machine instructions from a program; its output is the generated code. Protections such as stack canaries and pointer authentication are added here, so they cover only the code the compiler built with them.

A failure to convert between characters and bytes, for example an invalid multibyte or wide-character sequence. C's snprintf returns a negative value when one occurs, which is different from truncation.

The main release of Chrome and Chromium that ordinary users run, as opposed to the Beta, Dev and Canary test channels. Chromium's memory-safety statistics count security bugs that affected this release.
